title: Air-dry clay succulent pot with drainage
subtitle: A small round pinch pot sized for a single succulent, with a pressed drainage hole in the base
excerpt: A succulent pot is a pinch pot with a drainage hole pressed through the base before drying, sized to hold a 6 cm root ball. This version uses air-dry clay with no kiln. The finished pot is 8 cm across and 6 cm tall, sealed for decorative indoor use.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles. V&A open-access collection for ceramic plant pot form reference.

glossaryTerms.definition: A hand-building technique where a ball of clay is opened and thinned by pressing the thumb inside while rotating and pinching the walls upward
Fully air-dried and unfired; pale, lightweight, and fragile, ready for sealing
A raised ring of clay around the base of a pot that lifts the pot floor off the surface, allowing drainage to flow out freely
Clay that has dried to a firm, pliable state: stiff enough to hold its shape but still damp enough to accept surface tools or scoring.

content.text: A succulent pot is a small
pinch pot

with a drainage hole pressed through the base before drying, for housing a single small succulent with no risk of root rot. Air-dry clay needs no kiln. The finished pot is 8 cm across and 6 cm tall, sealed for indoor decorative use, and suited to plants in their own growing medium rather than bare-root planting.

materials.name: Acrylic varnish, matte (for final protective coat)
Small saucer or cork disc for catching drainage

content.text: Preparation

The drainage hole is pressed through the base before the pot is upright and the walls are thinned: this is the moment when the base is still flat and accessible. Have the needle tool within reach before you begin. Work on a canvas sheet or cloth-covered board. Keep a small bowl of water and a damp cloth beside you to keep your hands moist as you pinch: dry hands drag on the clay surface and cause cracks at the rim.
Opening the ball
Take 200 g of clay and roll into a smooth sphere between your palms. The ball should have no cracks or seams on the surface.
Hold the ball in your non-dominant hand. Press your dominant thumb into the centre to a depth of 3 cm. The hole should stop at least 15 mm from the base of the ball.
Widen the opening by rotating the ball in your hand while pressing the thumb outward against the inside. Work slowly, one quarter-turn at a time.
Pinching the walls
Pinch the walls between thumb inside and forefinger outside, working in rows from the base upward. Aim for a wall thickness of 6-7 mm throughout. Thinner walls are more likely to crack during
bone-dry
drying.

Keep the pot opening fairly upright as you work rather than letting it flare wide. Succulents do better in a pot that is taller than it is wide, so aim for a finished diameter of 8 cm and a height of 6 cm.
Smooth the interior walls with a damp pottery sponge after each row of pinching. This closes surface tears and compresses the clay, which strengthens the wall.
Even out the rim by pressing lightly with a flat wooden rib. The rim does not need to be perfectly level, but a roughly even top will look more considered.
Pressing the drainage hole

Turn the pot upside down and hold it steady. Locate the centre of the base. Press the needle tool through the base at 90 degrees to the surface, rotating it slightly as you push to make a clean hole rather than a rough tear. The drainage hole should be 8-10 mm in diameter.

Smooth the clay pushed up around the hole entrance on the interior base with a damp finger. The raised clay around the hole is useful: it creates a small raised lip that keeps the drainage hole from clogging against the saucer surface.
Turn the pot right-side up. Check the pot stands level. If it rocks, press a small circle of clay around the base exterior to create a
foot ring
: a raised ridge 3 mm tall around the base perimeter that also lifts the pot floor clear of the saucer so drainage flows freely.
Surface decoration
A succulent pot is a small
pinch pot

with a drainage hole in the base. Press the hole through before the clay dries. No kiln needed. The finished pot is 8 cm across and 6 cm tall. Seal it before use. Plant succulents in their own growing medium inside the pot.
Drying
Stand the pot upright on a canvas board to dry. Pinch pots dry faster than slab pieces because the walls are relatively thin. The pot passes through
leather-hard

in 12-24 hours at room temperature and reaches bone-dry in two to three days. The exterior will be pale and the piece will feel lightweight and no longer cool to the touch when fully dry. Check the drainage hole is still open at the leather-hard stage: if the hole has partially closed during drying, re-open it with the needle tool.
Finishing

Apply two coats of 50/50 PVA and water to all exterior surfaces and the rim. Leave the interior unsealed: PVA sealer can prevent the clay from breathing and may trap moisture in the root zone over time. Once the PVA is fully dry, paint the exterior with acrylics if desired. Apply a final coat of matte acrylic varnish over any painted surfaces to protect the decoration. Do not apply varnish to the interior.
Care

Air-dry clay is not fully waterproof even when sealed. This pot is suitable for succulents and cacti, which need infrequent watering. Each watering moistens the exterior clay through the drainage hole and through the walls to a small degree. The pot will soften if overwatered repeatedly: water succulents sparingly, allow the medium to dry out fully between waterings, and use a small saucer underneath to catch drainage and empty it promptly. Wipe the exterior with a dry cloth only. The pot is for indoor decorative use; do not leave outdoors in rain.
Variations
Make a set of three graduating pots from 100 g, 200 g, and 300 g balls of clay. Group them on a small tray or wooden board for a succulent arrangement.

Build a lip or collar at the rim by rolling a thin coil and attaching it to the rim at the leather-hard stage with score and slip. This adds definition and slightly increases the pot height without requiring more pinching.

Shape the pot into a faceted cylinder rather than a round form: press four or six flat panels against the exterior with the wooden rib while the clay is soft. Each facet is flattened with a single press, creating a geometric modern profile.

items.problem: Cracks appeared at the rim during pinching
items.cause: Hands too dry or clay drying between pinching passes
items.fix: Dampen hands before each round of pinching. Smooth the rim with a wet pottery sponge after every two or three rows of pinching to keep the rim moist and compress any forming cracks

items.problem: Base too thin and cracked through when the drainage hole was pressed
items.cause: The thumb was pressed too deep when opening the ball, leaving insufficient clay in the base
items.fix: Stop the thumb 15 mm from the base and work the walls rather than the base floor. A thicker base than you think you need is the right call: the base can be thinned from the outside later with a wooden rib

items.problem: Pot walls flared outward and the pot became a wide bowl rather than a taller pot
items.cause: Pinching the walls while the pot rested on its base encouraged the clay to spread downward and outward
items.fix: Hold the pot in the air rather than resting it on the board while pinching the upper walls. Keep the pot tilted so the opening faces sideways: gravity then helps pull the walls into a more upright position

items.problem: Drainage hole sealed over during sealing
items.cause: PVA was applied inside the pot and flowed into the drainage hole
items.fix: Re-open with the needle tool after the PVA is dry. Seal the exterior only and keep the pot interior uncoated
